title: A-R-V
hookLine: erev, evening; arev, sweet, and a guarantor: all Israel are guarantors

lines: I WILL BE SURETY FOR HIM.
cards: A father refuses to send his youngest son down to Egypt. He has already lost one boy; he won't risk Benjamin. But the family is running out of food.
Then Judah, an older brother, steps forward: "I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him." Put him on my account. If he doesn't come back, the blame is mine.
Later, in Egypt, when Benjamin is about to be kept as a slave, Judah steps forward again and offers to stay in his place. Today's root is the word under surety.

teach.b: A-R-V. Ayin, resh, vet. These letters carry more than one meaning.
First, evening: erev. The Torah's first day ends with it: "And the evening and the morning were the first day."
Evening is named before morning, and the rabbis read that as the reason a Jewish day, Shabbat included, begins in the evening.
Second, sweet: arev. A psalm says, "My meditation of him shall be sweet." And the blessing said before studying Torah asks God to make its words sweet in our mouths, with a word from these letters.

teach.h: AREV: THE ONE WHO STANDS SURETY.
teach.b: Third, the guarantor: arev again, the one who stands surety, the way Judah did for his brother.
The Talmud puts it in a single line: kol Yisrael arevim zeh ba-zeh, all Israel are guarantors for one another. In its setting it explains how one person can bear responsibility for another's wrong.
In its widest reading it says that nobody in the community is only on their own account. Fourth, side by side. These may be separate words that happen to share a spelling.
Some teachers set them together anyway: a day that begins in the dark, words that taste sweet, and people who answer for each other.
Judah's surety is where it gets concrete. He didn't promise to feel responsible. He put himself in the place where Benjamin would have stood.

how: Jewish days, Shabbat and festivals begin at evening, read from Genesis 1:5; the blessing before Torah study asks that its words be sweet; and the Talmud's principle 'all Israel are guarantors for one another' (Shevuot 39a) is cited for mutual responsibility.

games.q: you're Judah. in Egypt, the governor says Benjamin must stay behind as a slave. what do you do?
o: go home and tell your father the news.
offer to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place.
blame Benjamin for the cup in his sack.
games.why: "thy servant became surety for the lad": Judah asks to stay instead, so the boy can go home to his father.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose life touches yours, a child, a parent, a coworker who's struggling, a friend who's gone quiet, and see yourself standing beside them, the way Judah stood beside his brother.

Ask where you could put your name beside theirs, vouching for them, going with them to a hard appointment, speaking up for them in a room they aren't in, and hold that in mind. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

orig.note: Hebrew: a guarantor, one who stands surety; the same spelling means sweet, and erev, evening, shares the letters.

carryVoice: Your line: we stand surety. Judah said I will; the Talmud says all of us. Until tomorrow.
